title: Intel Foundry: How Better Power Delivery Could Unlock More AI Performance
gist: Daniel Nenni summarizes Intel Foundry's white paper on AI data-center power delivery: multi-kiloamp package currents make delivery losses a performance limiter, and Intel offers a menu of fixes (PowerVia on 18A, PowerDirect on 14A, Omni MIM, embedded capacitors, EMIB-T, and the C2VR capacitive regulator at 92% peak efficiency) so power delivery becomes a foundry-level design choice that frees facility power for compute.

insights.claim: AI accelerators can leave performance on the table despite more transistors, memory bandwidth and interconnect if their power delivery network cannot keep up.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Power delivery is becoming a differentiator in AI accelerator performance, not just process node.
insights.locator: An AI accelerator can have more transistors

insights.claim: Because AI accelerators run at low voltage, more power means more current; Intel's paper cites package currents in the multi-kiloamp range for highly integrated designs, and resistive losses rise with the square of current.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: I^2R scaling makes long delivery paths increasingly costly as accelerator power climbs.
insights.quote: Intel’s paper puts package currents in the multi-kiloamp range for highly integrated designs. Resistive losses rise with the square of current
insights.locator: AI accelerators operate at low voltages

insights.claim: Sudden current demand causes supply-voltage droops, so designers raise operating voltage to stay stable through dips, which increases energy consumption.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Better transient response directly reduces wasted voltage margin and energy.
insights.locator: Sudden jumps in demand can also cause

insights.claim: When compute chiplets and HBM share a package, power delivery competes with high-speed connections for routing and surface area, and each die can have different voltage and current needs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Package-level power solutions gain value as multi-die AI packages proliferate.
insights.locator: That challenge grows as compute chiplets

insights.claim: Intel's PowerVia on Intel 18A routes power through the back of the die, shortening current paths, reducing resistive drop and easing frontside routing congestion; Intel plans to build on it with PowerDirect on Intel 14A.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Backside power is a key Intel Foundry selling point for high-current logic customers.

insights.claim: Intel's Omni MIM uses vertical trenches to fit more on-die capacitance per area, and embedded capacitors add charge storage inside the package to cover sudden current demand while the regulator catches up.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Capacitance close to load addresses droop without raising voltage.
insights.locator: The paper also describes how to handle

insights.claim: Intel's EMIB-T adds vertical paths through the silicon bridge connecting dies, letting current take a more direct route through densely packed multi-die designs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: EMIB-T strengthens Intel's advanced packaging pitch for AI packages with HBM.

insights.claim: Intel's continuous capacitive voltage regulator (C2VR) replaces inductors with capacitors, can be thinned below 100 micrometers for potential placement beneath a compute die, and reached 92% peak conversion efficiency in the cited research design.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Under-die voltage regulation could disrupt conventional VRM placement and suppliers; note it is still a research design.
insights.quote: Intel reports a 92% peak conversion efficiency for the research design cited in the paper.

insights.claim: Placing voltage conversion directly under the load shortens the vertical path for low-voltage, high-current power and helps the regulator respond quickly to demand changes, which the author considers as interesting as the efficiency figure.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Placement, not only efficiency, is the key metric for next-gen integrated regulators.
insights.quote: The placement is as interesting as the efficiency figure.

insights.claim: At a fixed facility power budget, an accelerator that loses less energy between regulator and transistors leaves more power for computation and generates less heat, so modest gains across many accelerators can change how much compute fits within a rack's electrical and thermal limits.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Power-constrained data centers make delivery efficiency a compute-per-watt lever; gains depend on accelerator, workload and package.
insights.locator: Data centers have a finite amount

insights.claim: Intel Foundry's opportunity is offering designers a choice of where to gain: backside delivery for high-current logic, embedded capacitors or power-carrying bridges for crowded memory/chiplet packages, and under-die regulators for stacked designs.
insights.speaker: Daniel Nenni
insights.so_what: Positions power delivery as an Intel Foundry differentiation axis alongside transistor, memory bandwidth and packaging.
insights.quote: Having those options makes power delivery a design decision architects can make alongside transistor technology, memory bandwidth, and packaging.
